note: Source record for the 50-plant UK-favourites batch, 2026-08-10. Written by Claude (claude-opus-5) from general horticultural knowledge with no network access and no RHS lookup, then CORRECTED BY OSCAR on 2026-08-10 against his own sources — 26 plants amended, including 10 accepted-name changes and two Schedule 9 listings Claude had wrongly recorded as unrestricted. Values not touched by that pass remain Claude estimates. See VERIFY-QUEUE items 18-20. Fields kept here have no home in the card schema: foliage, container, hardinessNote, toxicity and the declared-uncertain list. Toxicity is folded into each card `resilience`; compliance rides `type` + `returnRisk`.

uncertain: Often sold as Prunus serrulata 'Kanzan'; RHS accepts the name as Prunus 'Kanzan'.
Surface roots can lift paving and lawns — allow real distance from hard landscaping.
Blossom is modest compared with ornamental cherries — this is bought for bark, and customers expecting a flowering cherry may be disappointed.

Crataegus laevigata 'Paul’s Scarlet'.hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK, including exposed and coastal sites.
uncertain: The double flowers set little or no fruit, so it carries far fewer haws than the plain species — a point for wildlife-minded customers.

Laburnum × watereri 'Vossii'.toxicity: All parts are poisonous if eaten and the seed pods are the most dangerous part. Advise against planting where young children play unsupervised.
uncertain: 'Vossii' sets far fewer seed pods than the species, which is why it is the form usually recommended — but it is not seedless and the toxicity warning still applies.

Acer palmatum 'Sango-kaku'.hardinessNote: Very hardy, but exposure and drying wind cause more damage than cold does.
uncertain: Stem colour is strongest on young wood and fades on older branches, so it needs occasional renewal pruning to keep the winter effect.
The winter leaf retention that sells beech hedging is a juvenile trait — it holds on clipped hedges and young trees, not on mature standards.

pestRisk 16 is deliberately high for a plant that is otherwise trouble-free: box tree moth is now widespread in England and blight is endemic. Customers should hear this before they buy a parterre's worth.

Prunus laurocerasus 'Rotundifolia'.hardinessNote: Hardy through most of the UK; hard winters can scorch foliage in exposed sites.
Prunus laurocerasus 'Rotundifolia'.toxicity: Leaves and seeds contain cyanogenic compounds and are harmful if eaten. Do not shred clippings in an enclosed space.
uncertain: Frequently planted as a quick screen and then resented for its size — the mature dimensions here are what it does if left, not what a clipped hedge holds at.
Semi-evergreen is honest: it holds most leaves in a mild winter and can strip in a hard one, which surprises customers sold it as evergreen.
Sold hard as a box alternative because it is immune to box blight and box tree moth, but it needs far more clipping to hold a crisp edge.

Laurus nobilis.hardinessNote: Hardy in milder and sheltered UK gardens; cold drying wind does more damage than frost alone.
Laurus nobilis.toxicity: The leaf is the culinary bay used in cooking; it is removed before eating rather than chewed.
uncertain: Bay sucker and scale are common on container-grown standards — the pestRisk here reflects clipped pot plants, not open-ground shrubs.
Pruning at the wrong time is the single most common reason a customer's forsythia stops flowering — it flowers on the previous year's wood.
The suckering habit is the main after-sale complaint; it is easily controlled but customers are rarely warned.

Magnolia stellata.hardinessNote: Very hardy; it is the early flowers that are frost-vulnerable, not the wood.
uncertain: The most reliably small magnolia and the usual recommendation for a small garden — but it is genuinely slow, so customers pay for size.
The flowers are sterile, so unlike the plain guelder rose it carries no berries — customers buying for wildlife should be told.

Viburnum davidii.toxicity: Berries are ornamental and should not be eaten.
uncertain: Plants are effectively dioecious: a lone specimen will not berry, and nurseries rarely sell them sexed. The blue berries are the main selling point, so this matters.
Goes bare-legged with age; customers should know it is meant to be cut hard rather than replaced.

Hypericum × hidcoteense 'Hidcote'.hardinessNote: Hardy through most UK gardens; may lose leaves in a hard winter.
uncertain: 'Hidcote' is sterile and sets no berries, unlike the berrying Hypericum inodorum types sold for cut stems.

Fuchsia 'Mrs Popple'.hardinessNote: Among the toughest hardy fuchsias. In colder gardens it behaves as a herbaceous plant, dying to the ground and reshooting in late spring.
Fuchsia 'Mrs Popple'.toxicity: Fuchsia berries are edible though not usually eaten.
uncertain: Late spring emergence causes customers to write it off as dead — the old top growth should be left on until growth shows.
The pink flowers clash with the orange young foliage — a well-known quibble, and some gardeners shear the buds off deliberately.

Hebe 'Red Edge'.hardinessNote: Hardy in milder and coastal gardens; cold inland winters on heavy soil are the risk.
uncertain: Hebe hardiness varies enormously across the genus; the small-leaved types like this are the tougher end, but H4 is a genuine ceiling.
It self-seeds freely via birds and is recorded as naturalised in parts of the UK and invasive in New Zealand — worth watching, though it carries no UK legal restriction.
Sold on a photograph of a coppiced mass planting; a single unpruned plant never looks like the picture, and that is the commonest disappointment.
SAPHYR is a trade series bred for scab and fireblight resistance; 'Cadange' is the cultivar denomination. Resistance is not immunity.

Listed on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. Sale is not banned; planting or causing it to grow in the wild is an offence. An earlier draft of this card wrongly stated it carried no Schedule 9 restriction — corrected by Oscar, 2026-08-10.
Dimensions are for the SHRUB form. It is also sold trained as a short climber, which is a separate card, not a size range on this one.
Frequently described as the most fragrant English rose.
Also widely sold as a climbing sport and as a half-standard; the dimensions here are for the bush form.
Its tolerance of a shaded or north wall is the reason it is still recommended after a century, but it flowers less freely there than in sun.

Rosa rugosa.hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy and the toughest rose in general cultivation.
Rosa rugosa.toxicity: Hips are edible and traditionally used for syrup; the irritant seed hairs are strained out.
uncertain: Listed on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. Sale is not banned; planting or causing it to grow in the wild is an offence, and the coastal habitats it escapes into are exactly where it is most often planted. An earlier draft of this card wrongly stated it carried no UK legal restriction — corrected by Oscar, 2026-08-10.

Lavandula angustifolia 'Hidcote'.hardinessNote: Hardy across the UK given sharp drainage; it is winter wet, not cold, that shortens its life.
uncertain: Skipping the annual August cut is the reason most lavenders go woody and split within five years — the plant does not recover from bare wood.

Salvia rosmarinus 'Miss Jessopp’s Uprigh.hardinessNote: Hardy in well-drained and milder gardens; cold wet clay is the reliable way to lose one.
Salvia rosmarinus 'Miss Jessopp’s Uprigh.toxicity: Culinary herb in normal kitchen quantities.
uncertain: RHS now places rosemary in Salvia as Salvia rosmarinus; the entire trade still labels it Rosmarinus officinalis, so both names should be searchable.

Hydrangea petiolaris.toxicity: Skin allergen; sap or handling may irritate sensitive skin. Harmful to dogs and cats if eaten.
uncertain: Notoriously slow for the first two or three years before it takes off — customers commonly return it as a failure in year two.
Adhesive pads mark render and paintwork when pulled off — sound brick and stone are fine, but this is the commonest complaint.
Unlike summer jasmine it is scentless — customers expecting jasmine perfume are regularly caught out.
The original 1862 hybrid and still the most-planted clematis in Britain. Group 3 pruning makes it the easiest large-flowered type to get right.
The self-seeding is the one thing customers should be warned about; shearing before seed sets prevents it entirely.

Hosta × tardiana 'Halcyon'.hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy; the crown is fully dormant in winter.
Hosta × tardiana 'Halcyon'.toxicity: Harmful to dogs and cats if eaten.
uncertain: The blue is a waxy bloom on the leaf surface, not a pigment — it rubs off and burns away in strong sun, which is why this needs shade to look like the label.

Heuchera villosa 'Palace Purple'.hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy and evergreen through UK winters.
uncertain: Seed-raised stock varies a lot in leaf colour, from good bronze-purple to disappointing green — vegetatively propagated plants are more reliable.
'Roma' is sterile, which is why it flowers so long and does not self-seed like the plain species — a genuine selling point over seed-raised astrantias.
Astilbes fail in ordinary borders far more often than they fail in shade — the limiting factor is moisture, not light.

Lamprocapnos spectabilis.toxicity: Harmful if eaten and the sap may irritate skin.
uncertain: Formerly Dicentra spectabilis and still widely sold under that name. Summer dormancy leads customers to dig it up by accident — it should be labelled in the ground.
Bought for the silver foliage, which is exactly the part that burns in sun — placement matters more than for most shade perennials.
Takes a year or two to establish and then runs; the same plant gets described as sulky and as invasive depending on how long the gardener has had it.

Crocosmia 'Lucifer'.hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK; the tallest and hardiest of the common crocosmias.
uncertain: Not to be confused with the invasive montbretia (Crocosmia × crocosmiiflora) naturalised in the west — 'Lucifer' is a well-behaved garden hybrid.

Agapanthus 'Northern Star'.hardinessNote: Among the hardiest agapanthus; deciduous types are far tougher than the evergreen ones.
uncertain: Deciduous vs evergreen is the single most useful thing to tell an agapanthus customer, and it is rarely on the label.

Verbena bonariensis.hardinessNote: Borderline in cold or wet gardens; it usually persists by self-seeding rather than by the original plant surviving.
uncertain: Frequently sold as a reliable perennial when it behaves more like a self-sowing biennial in much of Britain — worth saying honestly at the till.
The black seed cones are half the point — customers who cut it down in autumn lose the winter structure it is planted for.

Delphinium Black Knight Group.hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK; the plant survives cold easily, the spring shoots are what get eaten.
Delphinium Black Knight Group.toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten.
uncertain: Sold as a perennial but often behaves as a short-lived one; the Pacific Giant strains in particular are frequently treated as biennials.
Russell lupins are typically good for three or four years before they decline; customers expecting a permanent plant should hear that.
